content: Intimate partner violence (IPV) has significant negative impacts on individuals, their children, communities, and society as a whole, including economic and social consequences. Some governments and professional organizations recommend universal screening of all women for IPV in healthcare settings, rather than limiting inquiries to women who present with symptoms. This study aimed to evaluate whether screening for IPV in healthcare settings benefits women, improves outcomes such as identification, referral, and health measures, and whether it causes any harm. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and trial registries on February 17, 2015, to identify relevant studies. They included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed the effectiveness of IPV screening by healthcare professionals, either through direct face-to-face screening or by using the results of screening questionnaires. These were compared to usual care, which could include screening not involving healthcare professionals. Two authors independently assessed the risk of bias in the studies and extracted data. For binary outcomes, odds ratios (ORs) were calculated, while continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs), all with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The review included 13 trials involving 14,959 women from various healthcare settings, such as antenatal clinics, women’s health clinics, emergency departments, and primary care, primarily in high-income and urban areas. The overall quality of evidence was rated as low to moderate due to issues such as heterogeneity, risk of bias, and imprecision. Five studies were excluded from the primary analysis because they did not report identification data or did so in a way inconsistent with clinical identification by healthcare providers. In the remaining eight studies (10,074 participants), screening was found to increase the clinical identification of IPV victims or survivors (OR 2.95, 95% CI 1.79 to 4.87, moderate-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses showed that screening was particularly effective in antenatal care settings (OR 4.53, 95% CI 1.82 to 11.27, two studies, 663 participants), maternal health services (OR 2.36, 95% CI 1.14 to 4.87, one study, 829 participants), and emergency departments (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.03 to 7.19, three studies, 2,608 participants). However, no significant effect was observed in hospital-based primary care settings (OR 1.53, 95% CI 0.79 to 2.94, one study, 293 participants). Only two studies (1,298 participants) examined referrals to domestic violence support services following clinical identification, and no significant effect on referrals was detected (OR 2.24, 95% CI 0.64 to 7.86, low-quality evidence). Four studies (2,765 participants) investigated IPV prevalence but were excluded from the main analysis because the rates were not clinically recorded. These studies found no difference in IPV detection between face-to-face screening and computeror written-based assessments (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.36, moderate-quality evidence). Only two studies measured women’s experiences of violence three to 18 months after screening, and neither found evidence that screening reduced IPV. One study assessed women’s health outcomes at 18 months and found no differences. Although no adverse effects from screening interventions were reported, harm outcomes were only measured immediately after screening in most studies, with only one study reporting outcomes at three months. There was insufficient evidence to determine whether screening increased the uptake of specialist services, and no studies included an economic evaluation. In conclusion, while screening in healthcare settings increases the identification of women experiencing IPV, the overall rates of identification remain low compared to the estimated prevalence of IPV among women seeking healthcare. Pregnant women in antenatal settings may be more likely to disclose IPV when screened, but further rigorous research is needed to confirm this. There was no evidence of an effect on other outcomes, such as referrals, re-exposure to violence, health measures, or harm from screening. Therefore, while screening improves identification, there is insufficient evidence to support universal screening in healthcare settings. Future research should compare universal screening to case-finding approaches, with or without advocacy or therapeutic interventions, to better inform IPV identification policies and improve long-term outcomes for women.
